summary: Updates BGP Graceful Restart (RFC 4724) so the procedures can also be used when a BGP speaker receives a NOTIFICATION message or when the Hold Timer expires. It also defines a new Cease NOTIFICATION subcode for requesting a hard reset. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router is told to stop talking, its neighbors normally throw away everything it taught them. This update lets them keep using what they already know for a little while, like keeping a friend's phone number while they get a new phone.

questions: bgp graceful restart on hold timer expiry
what is the bgp hard reset subcode
what is the bgp stale timer
subtitle: Lets BGP routers keep forwarding through a session reset caused by an error, instead of throwing routes away.

tldr.problem: RFC 4724 Graceful Restart did not apply when a BGP NOTIFICATION message was sent or received, so a session reset for an error made reachability flap.
tldr.mechanism: A new Graceful Notification (N) bit in the Restart Flags field signals support. When both sides have exchanged it, NOTIFICATION messages and Hold Time expiry trigger Graceful Restart behavior, and a new Cease subcode, Hard Reset, requests a full session reset instead.
tldr.outcome: Speakers can keep forwarding while they restart a session to handle errors, and the stale timer becomes mandatory to bound how long old routes are kept.

facts.label: N bit position
facts.value: Second most significant bit of Restart Flags

today: RFC 8538 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2019. It updates RFC 4724, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Graceful Restart Needed Extending
sections.content:
For many classes of errors, BGP must send a NOTIFICATION message and reset the peering session. The Graceful Restart mechanism of RFC 4724 required the normal BGP procedures of RFC 4271 to be followed whenever a NOTIFICATION was sent or received. RFC 8538 updates RFC 4724 so that the Graceful Restart procedures can also run when a speaker receives a NOTIFICATION or the Hold Time expires.

The goal is to avoid flapping reachability and to keep forwarding while the speaker restarts the session to handle errors detected in BGP.

The RFC sums it up: when a session is reset, both speakers act as "Receiving Speakers" under RFC 4724, which means they retain each other's routes. The same holds for HOLDTIME expiry. Sending a Cease NOTIFICATION with the Hard Reset subcode defeats this and forces a full session reset.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, when two routers have a fight and hang up, they both forget what the other told them. Now they can hang up, keep the old directions for a bit, and call back.

sections.title: The Graceful Notification Bit
sections.content:
The Graceful Restart Capability carries a Restart Flags field. RFC 4724 defined its most significant bit as the Restart State (R) bit. RFC 8538 defines the second most significant bit as the Graceful Notification (N) bit.

A speaker shows that it supports the procedures in this RFC by advertising the Graceful Restart Capability with N set to 1. If a speaker that earlier advertised one set of Graceful Restart parameters opens a new session with a different set, the new parameters apply once the session reaches the ESTABLISHED state.
sections.plainLanguage: The N bit is a badge that says "I know the new rules". Both routers need to show the badge before the new rules are used.

sections.title: The Hard Reset Subcode
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new subcode for Cease NOTIFICATION messages, the Hard Reset subcode. Once the N bit has been exchanged, NOTIFICATION messages other than Hard Reset are called "Graceful", since they invoke Graceful Restart behavior.

A Hard Reset tells the peer the session is to be fully terminated. Its data portion holds an ErrCode, a Subcode and Data, using the IANA registries for BGP error codes and subcodes. In short, the Hard Reset encapsulates another NOTIFICATION message that explains the reason. On receiving a Hard Reset, a speaker MUST terminate the session following the standard procedures in RFC 4271.
sections.plainLanguage: A Hard Reset is a way of saying "this is a real goodbye, forget everything", with a note inside explaining why.

sections.title: Operation and the Receiving Speaker Rules
sections.content:
A speaker willing to send and receive NOTIFICATIONs under this RFC MUST advertise the N bit. Once it has received the N bit from its peer and gets a NOTIFICATION that is not a Hard Reset, it MUST follow the Receiving Speaker rules, and so must the speaker that generated the NOTIFICATION. After a HOLDTIME expiry, a speaker should generate the usual NOTIFICATION from RFC 4271 and then MUST follow the Receiving Speaker rules.

A speaker SHOULD NOT send a Hard Reset to a peer from which it has not received the N bit. The effect would still be a reset, since any NOTIFICATION results in one, but the peer might be unable to log the associated information. Once the session is re-established, both speakers SHOULD set their Forwarding State bit to 1. Otherwise, per Section 4.2 of RFC 4724, the routes will be flushed, defeating the purpose.

The RFC also edits the Receiving Speaker rules. The requirement that a route previously marked stale MUST be deleted, to handle consecutive restarts, now applies only if the N bit has not been exchanged. And the stale timer, which bounds how long stale routes are kept, goes from optional to required: an implementation MUST support a configurable stale timer. A suggested default is 180 seconds. It MAY be possible to disable the timer, giving infinite retention, but not by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Both routers keep the old map for a while, and they promise to throw it away after a set time so they do not follow a stale map forever.

sections.title: When to Send a Hard Reset
sections.content:
When to send a Hard Reset is an implementation-specific decision, but the RFC offers advice. Many Cease subcodes mean permanent or long-term termination, so Hard Reset suits them. The RFC lists subcodes 1 to 9 with suggested behavior: Maximum Number of Prefixes Reached, Administrative Shutdown, Peer De-configured and Hard Reset itself suggest a Hard Reset; Administrative Reset is left to user control; the others suggest a Graceful Cease.

These are suggestions, not requirements. The guiding principle is that if there is no realistic hope that forwarding can continue, or that the session will come back within the deadline, a Hard Reset should be used. For NOTIFICATION codes other than Cease, a Hard Reset does not appear to be indicated.

When used with RFC 8203 (Administrative Shutdown Communication), the outer Cease subcode MUST be Hard Reset, with the Administrative Shutdown or Administrative Reset subcode encapsulated inside. Network management reporting of a Hard Reset MUST use the error code Cease and the subcode Hard Reset. The RFC also warns that long or infinite retention time may cause operational issues and should be enabled with care.
sections.plainLanguage: If a neighbor is gone for good, say goodbye properly. If it is only a hiccup, keep the old directions and wait for it to come back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it does not change the basic security model of RFC 4724, except that protection against repeated resets is relaxed. An attacker could otherwise use repeated session resets to keep stale routes from ever being deleted. To reduce that risk, the stale timer is made mandatory, and the RFC notes that in practice it is already ubiquitous.

The RFC adds that this extension may modestly increase control plane resilience against denial of service, but that confounding and deployment-specific factors mean no general claims can be made.
sections.plainLanguage: Because routers now keep old directions after a hang-up, a troublemaker could keep hanging up. The timer makes sure old directions are thrown away in the end.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned subcode 9, Hard Reset, in the BGP Cease NOTIFICATION message subcodes registry. IANA also created a registry called "BGP Graceful Restart Flags" with bit 0 as Restart State (R, RFC 4724), bit 1 as Notification (N, RFC 8538) and bits 2 to 3 unassigned. A second registry, "BGP Graceful Restart Flags for Address Family", has bit 0 as Forwarding State (F) and bits 1 to 7 unassigned. Both use Standards Action as the registration procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The new badge and the new goodbye code were added to the official lists so nobody reuses them for something else.
